subtopic: Definition of a Limit and One-Sided Limits
stem: Consider the example \(f(x) = 3x + 1\), take \(a = 0\) and \(l = 1\). Verify the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition of the limit, i.e. find \(\delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - 0| < \delta\) implies \(|f(x) - l| < \varepsilon\).
solution:
[Textbook misprints (typography): the book sets the set-membership glyph \(\in\) throughout this section where the epsilon of the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition is meant — it prints a genuine \(\varepsilon\) later in this same block, confirming the intent — and writes "If fact any \(\delta \le \varepsilon/3\) will do" for "In fact".]

We want to find some \(\delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - 0| < \delta\) implies that \(|(3x + 1) - 1| < \varepsilon\)

if \(|3x| < \varepsilon\)  i.e. if \(3|x| < \varepsilon\)  i.e. if \(|x| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{3}\)

So, we can choose \(\delta = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{3}\)

(In fact any \(\delta \le \dfrac{\varepsilon}{3}\) will do.)

\(\therefore\ 0 < |x - 0| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - l| < \varepsilon\)

\(\therefore\ \lim_{x \to 0} (3x + 1) = 1\)
_note: Printed stem is only 'Consider the example f(x) = 3x + 1, take a = 0 and l = 1'; the instruction to verify the definition comes from the block's shared lead-in 'Strategy : Steps for verifying the ∈ - δ definition' printed above Ex. 1 — folded into the stem here so the question is self-contained. The book prints the set-membership glyph '∈' throughout this chapter where epsilon is meant (it prints a genuine ε in Ex. 6 of the 7.1.7 block, confirming the intent); transcribed as \varepsilon. The book also misprints 'If fact any δ ≤ ∈/3 will do' for 'In fact'. Fig. 7.2 sits below this example illustrating the band 1−∈ < y < 1+∈; it is illustrative and the example is answerable without it.

subtopic: Definition of a Limit and One-Sided Limits
stem: \(f(x) = x^2\). Here take \(a = 3\) and \(l = 9\). Find \(\delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - 3| < \delta\) implies \(|x^2 - 9| < \varepsilon\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the closing note says we must find the "lower bound" of \(|x + 3|\). To bound the product \(|x+3||x-3|\) ABOVE the argument in fact uses an UPPER bound, \(|x + 3| < 7\), which is what the derivation itself does. Only the word is wrong.]

We want to find some \(\delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - 3| < \delta\) implies \(|x^2 - 9| < \varepsilon\)

i.e. \(3 - \delta < x < 3 + \delta \Rightarrow |x^2 - 9| < \varepsilon\)

\(\delta\) can be chosen as small as we like and take \(\delta < 1\)

Then, \(3 - \delta < x < 3 + \delta \Rightarrow 2 < x < 4\) or \(5 < x + 3 < 7\)

We want \(|(x + 3)(x - 3)| < \varepsilon\)

But \(|(x + 3)(x - 3)| < 7|x - 3|\)

So \(7|(x - 3)| < \varepsilon \Rightarrow |x^2 - 9| < \varepsilon\)

If \(\delta = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{7}\), \(|(x - 3)| < \delta \Rightarrow |x^2 - 9| < \varepsilon\)

So we choose \(\delta = \min\left\{\dfrac{\varepsilon}{7}, 1\right\}\)

then \(|(x - 3)| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - 9| < \varepsilon\)

* Note that, we want to get rid of factor \(|x + 3|\). Hence we have to get its lower bound.
_note: The book's closing note says we must get the 'lower bound' of |x + 3|; to bound the product |x+3||x−3| ABOVE the argument actually uses an UPPER bound (|x + 3| < 7, from 5 < x + 3 < 7). The derivation itself is correct — only the word is wrong.

subtopic: Definition of a Limit and One-Sided Limits
stem: \(f(x) = [x]\), \(2 < x < 4\), where \([x]\) is the greatest integer function. Study the limits of \(f(x)\) as \(x \to 3\) and as \(x \to 2.7\).
solution:
[Textbook inconsistencies (two, neither affecting the answer): the stem gives the domain as \(2 < x < 4\) while the next line of the solution restates it as \(2 \le x \le 4\); and with \(\delta = 0.3\) the chain "\(2.7 + \delta < 3\)" reads \(3 < 3\), false as a strict inequality. Any \(\delta < 0.3\) repairs it, and the conclusion \(\lim = 2\) is correct either way.]

We have seen the \(f(x) = [x]\), \(2 \le x \le 4\)

Note that \([x] = 2\) for \(2 \le x < 3\)

\(= 3\) for \(3 \le x < 4\)

Let us study the limits of \(f(x)\) as \(x \to 3\) and \(x \to 2.7\)

\(\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = 3\),

But for \(x < 3\), \(f(x) = 2\). So, \(\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) = 2\).

If we take \(l = 3\), then for \(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and any \(\delta > 0\)

\(3 - \delta < x < 3 \Rightarrow f(x) = 2\) and \(|f(x) - l| = 1 \not< \varepsilon\)

If we take \(l = 2\), then \(3 < x < 3 + \delta \Rightarrow f(x) = 3\),

\(|f(x) - 2| = 1 \not< \varepsilon\)

\(\therefore\ \lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\) does not exist.

Consider \(\lim_{x \to 2.7} f(x)\)

Consider \(a = 2.7\). We see that for \(2 < x < 3\), \(f(x) = 2\).

If we choose \(\delta = 0.3\),

then \(2 < 2.7 - \delta < 2.7 < 2.7 + \delta < 3\)

and \(f(x) = 2\) is a constant.

\(\therefore\ \lim_{x \to 2.7} f(x) = 2\)
_note: Two printed inconsistencies. (1) The stem states the domain as 2 < x < 4 while the very next line of the solution restates it as 2 ≤ x ≤ 4. (2) With δ = 0.3 the chain '2.7 + δ < 3' reads 3 < 3, which is false as a strict inequality; any δ < 0.3 (or reading the interval as open) makes the argument correct, and the conclusion lim = 2 is right either way.

subtopic: Definition of a Limit and One-Sided Limits
stem:
Find left hand limit and right hand limit for the following function.

\(f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x + 1 & \text{if } x < 1 \\ 7x^2 - 3 & \text{if } x \ge 1 \end{cases}\)
solution:
Right hand limit, \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\), for \(x > 1\)

i.e. \(\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1} (7x^2 - 3) = 4\)

Left hand limit, \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\), for \(x < 1\):

\(\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1} (3x + 1) = 4\)

Since left and right-hand limits are equal, the two-sided limit is defined, and \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 4\).
_note: Printed as an unnumbered 'Example:' immediately after §7.1.6 (Existence of a limit of a function at a point x = a), with its own 'Solution :' — it carries no 'Ex. n' label, hence the ref number 1 assigned here.
The book prints no instruction word — the item reads 'Ex. 1 : lim … = lim …', the first '=' already beginning the solution. 'Evaluate' supplied so the stem is a question.

solution:
\(\lim_{x \to 1} \left( \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{x} - 1}{x - 1} \right) = \lim_{x \to 1} \left( \dfrac{\dfrac{1 - x}{x}}{x - 1} \right)\)

\(= \lim_{x \to 1} \left[ \dfrac{(1 - x)}{(x - 1) \times x} \right]\)

\(= \lim_{x \to 1} \left[ \dfrac{-(x - 1)}{(x - 1) \times x} \right]\)

\(= \lim_{x \to 1} \left[ \dfrac{-1}{x} \right]\)  \(\left[ \text{As } x \to 1,\ x - 1 \ne 0 \right]\)

\(= -\lim_{x \to 1} \left[ \dfrac{1}{x} \right] = -\dfrac{1}{1}\)

\(= -1\)

subtopic: Definition of a Limit and One-Sided Limits
stem:
Discuss the limit of the following function as \(x\) tends to 3 if

\(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + x + 1, & 2 \le x \le 3 \\ 2x + 1, & 3 < x \le 4 \end{cases}\)
solution:
As \(f(x)\) is defined seperately for \(x \le 3\) and \(x > 3\), we have to find left hand limit (when \(x \le 3\)) and right hand limit (when \(x > 3\)) to discuss the existance of limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x \to 3\).

For the interval \(2 \le x \le 3\); \(f(x) = x^2 + x + 1\)

\(\therefore\ \lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 3^-} (x^2 + x + 1) = (3)^2 + 3 + 1\)

\(= 9 + 3 + 1 = 13\)   -----(I)

Similarly for the interval \(3 < x \le 4\); \(f(x) = 2x + 1\)

\(\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 3^+} (2x + 1) = (2 \times 3) + 1\)

\(= 6 + 1 = 7\)   -----(II)

From (I) and (II), \(\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) \ne \lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x)\)

\(\therefore\ \lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\) does not exist.
_note: The book prints 'seperately' and 'existance'; transcribed as printed.

We can have \(\delta \le \dfrac{\varepsilon}{4}\) so that \(|(x - 1)| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - 7| < \varepsilon\)

[Textbook misprint: the compound-fraction step of the printed solution is labelled \(\lim_{x \to 5}\) where it must be \(\lim_{x \to 2}\) — every other line of the example, and its own bracketed remark, use \(x \to 2\). The value \(\frac{28}{5}\) is correct.]

\(\lim_{x \to 2} \left( \dfrac{x^7 - 128}{x^5 - 32} \right) = \lim_{x \to 2} \left( \dfrac{x^7 - 2^7}{x^5 - 2^5} \right)\)
